stem: Delphine, a collegiate gymnast, wrote her beam imagery script last winter, when she was first learning her acrobatic series. She runs it in her leotard beside the beam, and it lasts about as long as the series does. It goes from hand placement to hips to feet, the things she had to think about back then. "These days it's one long swing and I'm standing," she says. "The script makes me clumsy." Using the PETTLEP model, which change should the consultant suggest?
options: Environment: add the sights and sounds of a competition arena
Timing: run the images at the pace of the live series
Learning: rewrite the script around what she attends to now
Emotion: add the feelings she has when she competes
rationales: Arena detail would raise environmental equivalence, but her complaint is about which parts of the movement the script directs her to, not about where it seems to take place.
The script already lasts about as long as the series, so its pace matches. What no longer matches is its content.
The learning element asks that imagery change as the performer's skill changes. Her script still holds the part-by-part focus of a beginner, while she now performs the series as one flowing action.
Competitive feelings would suit images that seem flat or detached. She describes a script that breaks up a movement she now does as a whole, and adding emotion would leave that in place.
takeaway: Imagery scripts should be updated as skill develops, or they pull the performer back to an earlier stage.

stem: Tobias, an elite para swimmer, already uses imagery for his starts and turns. At major meets his warm-up splits are usually among the best of his season. Then his main rivals come out on deck. "I'm loose, I'm not flat, I know how I'm going to swim it," he tells the consultant. "But I look across at them and think, who am I kidding?" His splits fade from the first length. Which image should the consultant help him add?
options: Standing on deck beside his rivals, sure of himself and in command
Hearing the crowd behind the blocks as his energy starts to build
Swimming each length in the order and pace set by his race plan
Touching the wall first and seeing his name top the results
rationales: What drops is belief, and it drops when his rivals appear. Motivational general-mastery imagery, in which he sees himself confident and in control in that situation, matches that function.
Building energy is motivational general-arousal imagery. It would suit a swimmer who is too flat or too keyed up, and Tobias says he is neither.
Rehearsing a race plan is cognitive-general imagery. He knows how he will swim the race, so the plan itself isn't what fails him.

Picturing a specific result is motivational-specific imagery, which helps direct and energize effort toward a goal. His doubt strikes on deck, before any result, and the image doesn't have him facing it.
takeaway: Choose imagery by the function needed: mastery images for confidence and control in a demanding situation.

stem: Eleanor, a 61-year-old club golfer, has begun missing short putts to the left. Her partners still ask her to read greens for them, and they envy how unhurried she seems over the ball. Video from three rounds shows her wrists hinging just before contact, a habit her coach spent the spring replacing with a one-piece stroke. Over each putt she now says, "Come on, Ellie." Based on research matching self-talk to task demands, which phrase should she try over the ball?
options: "Dig in, one more good effort"
"Nice and easy, let it go"
"See the slope, pick the line"
"Shoulders rock, hands quiet"
rationales: Effort-focused self-talk is motivational and suits strength, power, and endurance. A short putt calls for precision, and effort isn't what is missing.
A calming phrase suits a player who is tense or rushed. She is unhurried over the ball, and her fault is in how the stroke is made.
Cueing the read would suit a player who misjudges line or pace. Her partners rely on her reads, so the trouble begins after she has picked the line.
Putting is a precision task, and the recurring miss comes from a specific technical fault. Short instructional self-talk tied to the one-piece stroke matches both the task and the problem.
takeaway: For precision tasks with a technical fault, short instructional self-talk fits better than motivational phrases.

stem: Kwame, a 16-year-old wrestler, has rated himself from 0 to 10 in the hour before each of his last four matches. Worry about the result has stayed at 1 or 2, and confidence at 8 or 9. "Pounding heart and shaking" has been 9 each time. His coach's notes say, "Arms like boards in the first period. Looks like himself by the second." Kwame agrees to learn one technique for that hour. Based on the matching hypothesis, which should the consultant teach?
options: Thought records, to test what he predicts about the match
Progressive muscle relaxation, to loosen him before he competes
Energizing imagery, to raise his activation before the whistle
Concentration cues, to bring his attention back to the mat
rationales: Thought records target anxious predictions. His worry ratings are very low and his confidence is high, so there is little for a cognitive technique to change.

His ratings and his coach's notes point to somatic anxiety without much worry. The matching hypothesis pairs bodily symptoms with a somatic technique, and progressive muscle relaxation addresses his rigid muscles.
Energizing would suit a wrestler who starts flat. His heart is already pounding, and more activation would add to the problem.
Attention cues suit a performer whose focus drifts. Neither the ratings nor the notes suggest that his mind is elsewhere; his body is.
takeaway: Match the technique to the symptoms: somatic methods for bodily anxiety, cognitive methods for worry.

stem: With players' agreement, a consultant trained in biofeedback has five professional esports players practicing with a heart rate variability display. For three weeks, each has done twenty minutes a day at six breaths per minute, and the software log confirms it. Two players now produce large, smooth waves. The other three hold the pace exactly, feel at ease, and still produce small, uneven ones. In resonance frequency training, what should these three players do next?
options: Practice during scrimmages with the display running
Practice for longer each day at the current pace
Try slightly faster and slower paces on the display
Try the current pace by feel with the display off
rationales: Moving into scrimmages suits players who can produce the pattern reliably in quiet practice. These three haven't produced it yet.
More time would suit players who have practiced little or are slowly improving. These three have practiced as planned at a pace that isn't producing the response.

Resonance frequency differs from person to person, near but not exactly at six breaths per minute. Good adherence with weak oscillations suggests this pace isn't theirs, so nearby rates should be tested for the largest heart rate swings.
Removing the display helps once a player can produce the pattern with it. Without feedback, these three would be repeating a pace that hasn't worked.
takeaway: In HRV biofeedback, the effective pace is individual: find the rate that yields the largest oscillations.

stem: Meera, a collegiate volleyball player, has used the same pre-serve routine for two seasons and can recite it without thinking. It runs from the referee's whistle to her toss: wipe the shoe, seven bounces, spin, breath, two looks, and more. Servers have eight seconds. On match video, her complete version takes about ten. On most serves she leaves something out, not the same thing twice, and those account for nearly all her errors. How should the consultant help her change the routine?
options: Rehearse it as it is until it runs on its own
Add a restart cue for times when play is delayed
Add a target choice and a quick image of the serve
Cut it down to two or three of its present steps
rationales: Rehearsal suits a routine that is new or half learned. After two seasons she has it by heart, and more practice won't make ten seconds fit into eight.
A restart cue suits a routine that is broken by delays. Her errors come on ordinary serves, when she is dropping steps to beat the clock.
Choosing a target and imaging can strengthen a thin routine. Hers already overruns the time allowed, and additions would make it longer.

The full routine can't be finished in the time the rules allow, so she improvises a different version each serve. Trimming it to a few steps gives her something she can repeat every time, and consistency is what makes a routine useful.
takeaway: A routine has to fit the time the task allows, or it cannot be consistent.

stem: Oskar, a violinist with a professional orchestra, has a featured solo next month. A phone rang during his last one. "Phones ring," he shrugs. The recording bears him out: not a flicker in his sound as it rings, about two seconds in all. Then for the next twelve bars the phrasing is ragged before it settles. A stand light that flashed in the spring left the same trace. On both recordings, everything before the incident is superb. Which skill should the consultant prioritize?
options: A rehearsed cue for picking up the music after a break in focus
Practice runs with staged noises until they cease to startle him
A settling routine to use in the wings before he walks on
A set of focus points to carry him through the long passages
rationales: Each incident is brief, but what follows isn't: he takes twelve bars to get back. A refocusing plan, such as a rehearsed cue that returns him to the music, targets the recovery.
Staged noise helps performers who are jolted by disturbances. His sound doesn't waver while the phone rings, so it's the aftermath that needs work.
A settling routine helps a performer begin well. He starts superbly, and the trouble comes in the middle of the piece.
Focus points help when attention drifts without prompting during long passages. His holds until an incident, and then he has trouble getting it back.
takeaway: When the distraction is brief but the disruption isn't, train the recovery.

stem: Ramón, a professional relief pitcher, is working with a consultant who uses the mindfulness-acceptance-commitment approach. Lately one sentence keeps arriving on the mound: "I'm a walk machine." His body feels fine, and he tracks the catcher's signs without trouble. But when the sentence shows up, he shakes off the fastball. "What's the point?" he says. "You don't throw one when you can't find the plate. That's just who I am this year." Which practice best fits what is happening?
options: Naming the qualities he wants to bring to each outing
Making room for tightness without trying to loosen it
Putting "I notice the thought that" in front of the words
Bringing his attention back to the ball each time it strays
rationales: Values work suits an athlete who has lost sight of what he wants to stand for. Here a particular thought is dictating which pitch he throws.
Acceptance of bodily discomfort suits an athlete who is fighting sensations. He says his body feels fine.
He takes the sentence as a fact about himself and chooses pitches by it, which is cognitive fusion. Prefacing it as a thought is a defusion practice that lets him see it as words he need not obey.
Present-moment practice suits an athlete whose attention wanders. He follows the signs without trouble and then acts on the thought.
takeaway: When a thought is treated as fact and drives behavior, defusion is the process to train.

stem: Renata, a regional sales director, wants hers to be the company's top region. On mornings when the leaderboard refreshes, she studies it until lunch, along with a chart of her own revenue, and on those days she logs about half her usual client calls. "In my best quarters I just called people," she tells the consultant. "It's no mystery what works." The ranking will stand as her aim for the year. Which goal should anchor her days for the next month?
options: Outcome goal: finish ahead of the two regions nearest hers
Performance goal: beat her own revenue from last quarter
Learning goal: find three better ways to win new accounts
Process goal: reach six clients by phone each day
rationales: Another ranking goal gives her more to watch. It depends on other regions, and watching standings is what is displacing her calls.
Beating her own revenue is more controllable than a ranking, but it's a result she is already checking in place of working.
A learning goal suits someone who doesn't yet know how to succeed at a complex task. She knows what works.
She knows the behavior that brings results and drops it when she watches numbers. A process goal puts her attention and effort back on an action she controls.
takeaway: When watching results crowds out effective action, anchor the day with process goals.

stem: Fire crews have just finished a live-fire scenario in which they practiced a breathing-and-refocus skill. Back outside, the consultant asks how it went, and for fifteen minutes they tell it in turn: who lost the count on the stairs, who found it again at the door, what the heat did to their patience. When the stories run out, the training captain says, "Good. Now everybody pick one thing to do on your next call." Following Kolb's cycle, what should the consultant have the crews do at this point?
options: Go around again for what each person noticed and felt
Work out when the skill holds and when it breaks down
Choose one way that they will use the skill on a call
Run the scenario once more with positions exchanged
rationales: Noticing and feeling belong to reflective observation, and the crews have just spent fifteen minutes on it until the stories ran out.
The crews have had the experience and reflected on it. Abstract conceptualization comes next in Kolb's cycle: drawing a general understanding from the accounts, which then informs what they try.
Choosing what to try is active experimentation. The captain's suggestion skips the step in which the stories become an idea worth trying.
Another run is a new concrete experience. It would come after crews have drawn a conclusion from this one and have something to try.
takeaway: Kolb's cycle runs experience, reflection, conceptualization, experimentation; a lesson needs drawing out before it is applied.

stem: A consultant is following Carron and Spink's protocol in a workshop for the coaches of a U14 girls' soccer club. The head coach opened by describing what a close-knit team had done for her last squad. The coaches have just finished sorting moments from their season under environment, structure, and processes, and they sorted them well. "So," the consultant asks, "what will Thursday's practice look like?" They glance at one another. Which step comes next?
options: Have the coaches come up with strategies for this team
Show the coaches how cohesion can benefit a team
Take the coaches through the factors that shape cohesion
Have the coaches carry out strategies at regular practices
rationales: They value cohesion and can use the framework, but have no plan for Thursday. The practical stage comes next, when leaders generate specific strategies for their own group.
Showing the benefits is the introductory stage. The head coach's opening story suggests that this has been covered.
Explaining the factors is the conceptual stage. The coaches have just sorted their own examples correctly, so they have the framework.
Carrying out strategies is the intervention stage. Their glances at one another show that they don't yet have strategies to carry out.
takeaway: Carron and Spink's protocol moves from introductory to conceptual to practical to intervention.

stem: Yuki, a 15-year-old figure skater, images her free skate every night. At the consultant's request, she raises a hand at the opening step and again at the final pose. The consultant's note reads "6 min 10 sec" for a program that lasts under four. "I stay with each jump until I like it," she explains. Her competition film shows clean technique, yet by the second half she is reaching her jumps ahead of the music. Using the PETTLEP model, which change should the consultant suggest?
options: Perspective: watch the program from the judges' side
Timing: run the images at the pace of the live program
Learning: rework the images around her present skill
Physical: image while standing in her skates and dress
rationales: An external view can help with body shape, but her technique on film is clean. Her jumps are out of step with the music.
She images the program at well over its real length and skates it out of time. PETTLEP's timing element calls for imagery at the pace of performance, especially when tempo is part of the skill.
Reworking content suits a skater whose images lag behind her skill. Nothing suggests that what she images is out of date; it's how long it lasts.
Skates and dress would raise physical equivalence, but they wouldn't bring a six-minute image in line with a four-minute program.
takeaway: When pace and rhythm matter, imagery should run in real time.

stem: An elite women's rugby sevens squad learned three new restart plays this week and flies to a tournament on Friday. The coach wants more rehearsal without more running. The consultant watches a session: handling is crisp, the mood is upbeat, and nobody looks rattled when a play is blown dead. Twice, though, the jumper goes up for one call while the players outside her set off for another, and they stand laughing in the wrong places. Which imagery should the consultant give the squad?
options: Imagery of the catch and pass, felt through the hands
Imagery of the squad's energy lifting at the whistle
Imagery of staying assured when a restart goes astray
Imagery of the runs and choices that go with each call
rationales: Imaging a skill such as the catch is cognitive-specific. Handling was crisp, so the skills aren't what needs rehearsal.
Raising energy is motivational general-arousal imagery. The mood was upbeat, and the plays broke down for another reason.
Staying assured is motivational general-mastery imagery. Players took the failed plays in stride, so composure is in place.
Players were following different calls, so what needs rehearsal is the plan. Cognitive-general imagery covers strategies: who goes where, and what to choose on each call.
takeaway: Use cognitive-general imagery to rehearse strategies and plays, and cognitive-specific imagery for skills.

stem: Jonah, a soldier preparing for a selection course, loses pace in the last miles of long loaded marches. An instructor who reviewed the film says his stride and posture at mile eighteen could be spliced into mile two. He has yet to miss a checkpoint. On the one march when a friend walked beside him shouting, he held his pace to the end. Asked what he tells himself late in a march, he says, "That I'm done." Which self-talk should he practice for those miles?
options: "I've got this, keep driving"
"Short steps, chest over hips"
"Check the map, check the bearing"
"Drop the jaw, breathe out slow"
rationales: His form holds and he finds his way, but his effort fades and revives with encouragement. For an endurance task limited by effort, motivational self-talk is the match.
Technical cues suit a breakdown in form. Film shows that his stride and posture late in the march are the same as early on.
Navigation cues suit someone who loses the route. He has yet to miss a checkpoint.
Calming cues suit someone who is too tense or keyed up. Shouting helped him hold his pace, so his difficulty isn't too much activation.
takeaway: When effort, not technique, limits an endurance task, motivational self-talk fits.

stem: Gabriel, a startup founder, pitches to investors next month. In the week before each pitch, he drafts emails apologizing to his staff for the funding they won't get. "They'll walk out by the third slide," he tells the consultant, which is what he said before the last four pitches, two of which were funded. As he says it, he is sprawled in his chair, yawning. Colleagues say that on the day he is lively and fields interruptions with ease. Applying the matching hypothesis, which technique fits best?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation, done each evening that week
Upbeat music and movement, done just before he presents
Thought records, comparing his forecasts with what occurs
Distraction training, presenting through staged interruptions
rationales: Muscle relaxation targets bodily tension. He is sprawled and yawning as he describes his fears, so his anxiety isn't showing up as tension.
Energizing suits a performer who is flat on the day. Colleagues say he is lively when he presents.

His anxiety takes the form of predictions that his own record contradicts, with little bodily arousal. The matching hypothesis pairs cognitive anxiety with a cognitive technique, and thought records test his forecasts.
Distraction training suits someone thrown by interruptions. He fields them with ease.
takeaway: Worry without bodily arousal calls for a cognitive technique.

stem: A county EMS agency is adding a paced-breathing skill for paramedics. Interest is high: medics asked for the training, and many can explain what slow breathing does to heart rate. At the end of the first workshop, seated in a silent classroom, they tried it for two minutes without the instructor's count. Three of twenty held the pace. The operations chief has booked the simulator for next week and is eager to move. What should the next phase consist of?
options: Repeated practice in the classroom
Practice during simulated high-stress calls
A lesson on how slow breathing works
Prompted use on live calls, logged afterward
rationales: Most medics can't yet produce the skill in an easy setting. It should be learned to a dependable level in calm conditions before stress is added.
Simulation is the place to test a skill that medics can already do. In a silent room, seventeen of twenty couldn't hold the pace, so the simulator is a step too soon.
Education suits medics who doubt the skill or don't know its purpose. They asked for it and can explain how it works.
Live use is the last step in the progression, after the skill holds up in practice and simulation.
takeaway: Build a self-regulation skill in calm settings first, then under simulated stress, then on the job.

stem: Paloma, a 17-year-old tennis player, tends to lose several points in a row after an unforced error. On match video she turns away from each miss, strolls along the baseline with a long breath out, and bounces the ball four times, the picture of ease. The consultant stops the video at the start of six lost points and asks what she had in mind for each. "Um, getting it back in?" Yet away from the court she can talk through opponents' weaknesses in detail. What should her between-point routine gain?
options: A gesture that marks the last point as finished
A slow breath that brings her arousal back down
A choice about how to play the coming point
A fixed sequence that readies her to start play
rationales: A gesture suits a player who is still caught up in the miss. She already turns away from it and looks at ease.
A slow breath suits a player who remains wound up. She already takes one, and by the next point she is relaxed.
She has tactical knowledge but begins points without using it. Planning the coming point is the piece that her between-point time lacks.
A starting ritual suits a player whose preparation is haphazard. She bounces the ball four times before each point.
takeaway: Between points, recovering from the last one is only half the job; the next one needs an intention.

stem: Zuri, a professional soccer goalkeeper, keeps conceding on quick counterattacks that begin at the far end. Reviewing one, the consultant asks what she saw while her team was still attacking. She recounts the opposing midfielder's every touch before the long pass. Asked where her own fullbacks were, she can't say, and the runner who scored "came from nowhere." It is the same for the next three goals. In Nideffer's terms, which focus should she practice for those spells?
options: Narrow-external, locked onto the ball
Broad-internal, thinking through what could come
Narrow-internal, checking her breathing and stance
Broad-external, taking in the whole of the field
rationales: Locking onto the ball is what she does now. She can recall each touch, and that focus is costing her the rest of the field.
A broad-internal focus is for analysis and planning. The goals came from runners she didn't see, and thinking would take attention further from the field.
Checking her own body suits a performer who needs to steady or center herself. Nothing suggests tension; she is missing what is around her.
She can describe the ball but not her fullbacks or the scorer, a focus too narrow for the demands of the moment. A broad-external focus lets her read the whole situation as it develops.
takeaway: Match attentional width to the moment: reading open play calls for a broad-external focus.

stem: Anouk, a corps de ballet dancer working with a consultant in an acceptance and commitment approach, hasn't auditioned for a soloist part in two seasons. "My stomach will flip, and my head will announce that I'm going to freeze," she says, smiling. "They can come along. I used to fight them every class." She dances, she adds, to say something to an audience, and soloists get to. The audition form is still in her bag, blank. "One of these days," she says. What should the consultant do now?
options: Help her clarify what matters to her about dancing
Help her commit to a step and to a date for it
Help her watch the thought of freezing as just words
Help her make room for what she feels in her body
rationales: Clarifying values suits someone unsure what she wants her dancing to stand for. She has just put it into a sentence.
She knows her values and is willing to have the thoughts and feelings, but she hasn't acted. Committed action is the missing process, and the blank form is an obvious first step.
Defusion suits someone ruled by the thought. She describes her head's announcement with a smile and no longer fights it.
Acceptance suits someone struggling against sensations. She has stopped fighting them and says they can come along.
takeaway: When values are clear and willingness is present, ACT turns to committed action.

stem: Kiran, a collegiate swimmer, has two process goals: hold a tight streamline to the flags off every wall, and breathe every third stroke. "Those are exactly what I need," he says, and his coach sees him working at them daily. A month in, the consultant asks how many walls he hit that morning. "Half, maybe?" Underwater video shows about one in five, the same as each week so far. What should the consultant do?
options: Make the goals harder, so that they ask more of him
Drop one goal, so that he can attend to the other
Give him a regular count of how often he meets them
Talk over why the goals matter, so that he commits
rationales: Harder goals suit someone who is meeting them comfortably. He is meeting this one about one time in five.
Fewer goals suit someone who is overloaded. Two isn't many, and what he lacks is an accurate sense of how he is doing.
He is committed and trying, but believes he is doing far better than he is. Goals work when people get feedback on progress, and a regular count would let him adjust.
Discussing their importance suits someone who is lukewarm. He says they are what he needs and works at them daily.
takeaway: Goals need feedback: without it, committed people can't tell whether to adjust.

stem: A national wheelchair rugby program runs a six-part focus workshop by video call, and pays for two hours of the consultant's time a week. Attendance so far is twelve, then eight, then five. Those who come stay to the end, talk over one another, and try every exercise. Apologies from the rest say much the same thing: club training has started, on different evenings in every city, and could they get what they missed? How should the consultant deliver the remaining parts?
options: As live calls built around practice in breakout rooms
As live calls cut to about half their present length
As one-to-one video calls with each of the athletes
As recorded lessons with practice tasks for each week
rationales: Breakout practice suits calls on which athletes are passive. Those who attend are already active; the others can't be there.
Shorter calls suit athletes who tire or drift. Those who come stay to the end, and a shorter call at the same hour would still clash.
Individual calls suit athletes whose needs differ. Here they want the same material, and twelve calls won't fit into two hours a week.
Athletes value the material but share no free evening. Recorded lessons with practice tasks let them keep taking part around their own schedules.
takeaway: Choose the virtual format that removes the actual barrier, whether that's engagement, fatigue, or scheduling.

stem: A consultant is asked to lead team building with a collegiate lacrosse squad at midseason. The men are fond of one another, show up early, and have a strong sense of who they are as a program. In film sessions, though, two defenders argue over a goal that each thought was the other's to stop. A reserve tells the consultant, "I warm up, I stand there. I'd do whatever they wanted if I knew what it was." Within Carron and Spink's framework, what should the intervention target?
options: Group structure: members' roles on the team
Group structure: shared norms for behavior
Group processes: team goals and sacrifices
Group environment: distinctiveness and closeness
rationales: The defenders and the reserve don't know what is expected of them in particular. Role clarity and acceptance are part of group structure, and they are what both examples point to.
Norms concern standards expected of the whole team. Players already show up early, and the confusion is about who does what.
Goals and sacrifices suit a team that lacks common aims or willingness to give things up. The reserve says he would do whatever was wanted.
Distinctiveness and closeness suit a team that doesn't feel like one. These players are fond of one another and know who they are as a program.
takeaway: Arguments over whose job it is, and idle reserves, often signal unclear roles.

stem: Valentina, an elite karate athlete, competes in kata and pictures each form through her own eyes before she performs. Judges praise her timing and balance. Marks come off for a trailing arm that drops behind her and a back knee that bends. "I'm stunned every time I get the sheet," she says. "In there it's perfect." She wants her imagery to help with those two faults. Which image should the consultant have her add?
options: The view ahead of her as she moves through the form
The feel of her weight shifting from stance to stance
The sound of her breath and steps marking the rhythm
The sight of the form as an onlooker would see it
rationales: The view ahead is the internal perspective that she uses now. A dropped arm behind her is out of that picture.
Kinesthetic images of shifting weight support balance, which judges already praise.
Auditory images support rhythm, and her timing is praised too.
Her faults are in body shape that can't be seen through her own eyes. External visual imagery is well suited to form-based skills because it shows the positions being judged.
takeaway: External visual imagery helps when body shape matters and can't be seen from the inside.

stem: Brianna, a 16-year-old softball pitcher, is new to imagery. Asked to describe a session, she says she can see the red stitching, smell the dirt, and feel the ball roll off her fingers as she looks in at the mitt. "And then it sails over the catcher. I try to bring it down and it sails again. I sit there, totally calm, throwing wild pitches." She'd like to keep at it. What should the consultant have her work on?
options: Adding sights, sounds, and feelings to the pitching scene
Steering simple images, such as a ball rolling to a stop
Picturing the same pitch from the catcher's point of view
Relaxing for a few minutes before the pitching scene
rationales: Added detail builds vividness. Her scene is already rich in sight, smell, and feel.
Her images are vivid but don't do what she intends, which is a lack of controllability. Practice in manipulating simple images, then harder ones, builds that ability.
Another viewpoint would change what she sees, but the ball would still not go where she sends it.
Relaxation suits someone too tense to image. She describes herself as totally calm.
takeaway: Vividness and controllability are separate imagery abilities; train the one that is missing.

stem: Lucan, a wheelchair basketball player on a development squad, reads his free-throw imagery script to the consultant. It has the glare on the backboard, the hum of the crowd, two seconds left, his team a point down, and what the win would mean. "I get goosebumps," he says. The consultant asks how the shot itself goes. He closes his eyes and runs it for as long as a real one takes. "I don't know. It just goes up." What should the script gain?
options: The drive through his shoulders and the ball leaving his fingers
The sights and sounds around him as he sets up for the shot
The importance of the moment and the emotion that it stirs
The pace of the shot, so that it unfolds as fast as a real one
rationales: The setting and meaning are rich, but the act is missing from his image. Kinesthetic detail of his own movement would make it resemble the shot that he performs.
The surroundings are already there: the glare, the hum, and the clock.
The stakes are there too, and they give him goosebumps.
His image lasts as long as a real shot, so it's already running at the right pace.
takeaway: Good imagery includes the performer's own responses, not just the scene.

stem: Arlo, a 15-year-old diver, and his consultant are working through cognitive restructuring. His log shows the same sentence before most competitions: "I always mess up my reverse at big meets." This week he brought his results and went through them aloud: clean, clean, missed, clean, missed, clean. He looked up. "Huh. Not always, then." His next big meet is three weeks away. What should come next?
options: Log the thoughts that come up at his coming meets
Weigh the sentence against how his dives have gone
Word a new sentence that fits what he has found
Rehearse a replacement sentence before his dives
rationales: Logging identifies the thoughts to work on. His log has already shown the one that recurs.
Weighing the sentence against his record is what he has just done, and he has drawn the conclusion himself.
He has identified the thought and tested it. The next step is to form a more accurate alternative in words that he believes.
Rehearsal comes once there is something to rehearse. He has found the old sentence wanting, but hasn't yet put anything in its place.
takeaway: Restructuring runs in order: identify the thought, test it, form an accurate alternative, practice it.

stem: Ines, a collegiate high jumper, wants a cue word for the last strides of her approach. Her consultant and coach watch film of twenty jumps with her. On the good ones she is tilted well away from the bar through the curve. On the misses she is upright by the third-last stride and runs almost straight at the bar, though her speed, knee lift, and expression look the same on every jump. Which cue should she try?
options: "Pop," to sharpen the lift of her knee
"Lean," to hold her body angle on the curve
"Float," to ease tightness from her stride
"Charge," to bring more speed to the bar
rationales: A takeoff cue suits a jumper whose knee lift fails. Hers is the same on makes and misses.
Body angle through the curve is what separates her makes from her misses. A short instructional cue tied to that feature directs her attention to the thing that matters.
An easing cue suits a jumper who tightens up. Nothing on film suggests tension on the misses.
A speed cue suits a jumper who slows down. Her speed doesn't change.
takeaway: A good cue word points to the feature that separates good attempts from poor ones.

stem: Odalys, a professional opera singer, began with full progressive muscle relaxation and has worked down from sixteen muscle groups to four. Last week the consultant asked her to skip the tensing and simply let go. She did, and within two minutes she was as relaxed as ever; a week of home practice has gone the same way. Between scenes she has perhaps twenty seconds in the wings. What should she practice next, at home?
options: Pairing a silent word with each exhale once she is relaxed
Tensing and releasing a smaller number of muscle groups
Letting go of her muscles without tensing them beforehand
Relaxing while she moves about and sings her lines
rationales: She can release without tensing, but it takes two minutes and she has seconds. Cue-controlled relaxation, which links the relaxed state with a word and the breath, is the next step toward a quick version.
Fewer groups is the abbreviated stage. She has been through it, down to four groups.
Release-only practice is the stage that she has just spent a week on, and it works.
Relaxing while active is differential relaxation, which builds on a relaxed state that she can call up quickly. She can't do that yet.
takeaway: Relaxation training shortens in stages: full, abbreviated, release-only, then cue-controlled.

stem: Fergus, a professional golfer, has had eight weeks of heart rate variability biofeedback in a consultant's office. In each of the last five sessions the wave on the display turned smooth within a minute of his sitting down. On Saturday, playing nine holes with friends, he tried the breathing and "had nothing." The consultant asks how he can tell, in the office, that he has found the rhythm. He points to the screen. How should the next sessions run?
options: More practice, with the display in full view
Practice under mild stressors, with the display on
Practice on quiet holes, with no equipment
Practice with the display hidden, checked afterward
rationales: More of the same suits a golfer who hasn't yet produced the pattern reliably. He has, five sessions running.
Stressors suit a golfer who can find the rhythm on his own when calm. He still needs the screen to tell him that he has it.
Quiet holes suit a golfer who can produce the rhythm without the display. He tried an easy round with friends and couldn't.
He depends on the screen and has no internal sense of the rhythm. Removing the display while still recording lets him learn to feel it before taking the skill elsewhere.
takeaway: Feedback should be faded so that the performer learns to sense the skill without it.

stem: A professional basketball team recorded its weaker free-throw shooters, with their agreement, in pressured drills. Makes and misses look alike in most respects: the same seconds spent at the line, the same arm angles, nearly the same heart rate. The eye tracker shows one gap. Before makes, players' eyes come to rest on the front of the rim for almost a second. Before misses, they arrive there from the ball or backboard just as it is released. What should these players train?
options: A set sequence of actions from receiving the ball to release
A steady look at one spot that starts earlier in the shot
A breathing skill that lowers arousal as they step to the line
A cue phrase that guides the arm through the shooting motion
rationales: A set sequence suits shooters whose preparation varies. Their time at the line is the same on makes and misses.
The makes have a longer final fixation on the target before release, the quiet eye. Training an earlier, steadier final gaze targets the one thing that separates makes from misses.
Breathing suits shooters who are over-aroused on misses. Heart rate hardly differs.
A technical cue suits shooters whose motion changes on misses. Arm angles are the same.
takeaway: Quiet eye training lengthens the final steady fixation on the target before the movement.

topic: Choosing a technique for the moment
stem: Eli, a 12-year-old BMX racer, horses around with friends in the staging area and rides the straights as well as anyone. His starts are another matter. On helmet video, he rolls into the gate, sets his pedals, and within three or four seconds, as the cadence begins, his knuckles whiten and his head turns to the riders on either side. He leaves half a bike length behind. Which technique best fits what he needs?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation before he goes to the gate
Imagery of a clean lap while he waits to be called up
Centering on a single breath and a cue word in the gate
Upbeat music in the staging area until his helmet is on
rationales: Muscle relaxation beforehand suits a racer who arrives tense. In the staging area he is horsing around.
Lap imagery suits a racer unsure of the course or of himself on it. He rides it as well as anyone.
Tension and lost focus both arrive in the few seconds before the start. Centering takes a breath, lowers tension, and directs attention to a start cue, so it fits the moment and the problem.
Music suits a racer who is flat before his race. He is lively, and the trouble comes later.
takeaway: Centering fits when tension and lost focus strike in the last seconds before action.

stem: A national swimming academy asks a consultant for help with resilience among its 15- to 18-year-olds. Race simulations are frequent and the sets are brutal. "That's why we came here," the swimmers say, and their times are improving. But one learned she had been cut from a relay by reading a list on a door. Others hide sore shoulders or a bad week from the coaches, who say they save the talking for nationals. Which change best fits research on building resilience?
options: Raise the challenge, and keep support where it is
Keep the challenge where it is, and raise support
Raise the challenge and the support side by side
Lower the challenge, and keep support where it is
rationales: More challenge suits a place where people are well supported but seldom stretched. These swimmers are already tested hard.
Demands are high and welcomed, but swimmers face setbacks without help and hide difficulties. Resilience develops when high challenge is matched by high support, and support is what is missing.
Raising both suits a stagnant setting with little of either. Challenge here is plentiful.
Less challenge suits swimmers who are overwhelmed despite good support. These ones like the hard work and are improving, and they lack support.
takeaway: Resilience grows where high challenge meets high support; change whichever one is lacking.

stem: Five days before the conference tournament, a collegiate basketball coach who has been reading about mindfulness asks the team's consultant to "bring the guys something on Monday." The team has used a breathing-and-refocus routine since October. The consultant's chart for the last three games shows it at almost every dead ball, and players say it "just happens now." No one has asked for extra help. What should the consultant recommend for the week?
options: Introduce one short mindfulness exercise on Monday
Run a refresher on the routine at Monday's practice
Offer individual sessions to players during the week
Leave the routine as it is through the tournament
rationales: A new exercise suits preseason, when there is time to learn it. Five days out, it could distract from a routine that is working.
A refresher suits players who have let the routine slip. They use it almost everywhere, and reviewing something automatic may draw attention to its parts.
Individual sessions suit a week when some players report trouble. No one has.
The skill is automatic, used, and valued. Just before competition, trust in well-practiced skills does more good than something new, and mindfulness can be planned for the off-season.
takeaway: Close to competition, protect well-learned skills and save new ones for later.

stem: A recreational hockey coach has fifteen minutes for a consultant to teach her 8- to 10-year-olds a relaxation game, with parents watching. During shootouts, she says, the skaters lock their knees and grip their sticks so hard that she has to pry their fingers open. "They have no idea they're doing it. 'I'm loose, Coach!'" She would like them to be able to tell for themselves. Which game best fits?
options: "Statues": stand still and listen for the softest sound
"Balloons": breathe in big, then let the air out slowly
"Robots and spaghetti": go stiff all over, then floppy
"Movies": close your eyes and visit a favorite quiet place
rationales: A listening game trains attention. The children's need is to notice what their muscles are doing.
Balloon breathing can calm and is easy for this age, but it teaches them little about the difference between a tight grip and a loose one.
The children don't recognize muscle tension. Alternating stiff and floppy is a child-sized form of progressive muscle relaxation, which teaches the contrast between tension and release.
A quiet-place image suits children who are worried or upset. These ones think that they are loose when their bodies aren't.
takeaway: Progressive muscle relaxation, turned into a game, teaches children to feel the difference between tense and loose.

stem: A collegiate soccer player has given written consent for her consultant and her athletic trainer to share what she is working on with each. In the consultant's office she can drop her shoulders and breathe out on cue in seconds, and she uses the skill before exams. During daily range-of-motion exercises for her knee, though, she clenches and holds her breath. "Once the bending starts, it goes clean out of my head." The consultant is on campus on Fridays. What should the consultant do?
options: Attend her rehabilitation and cue the skill there
Go over the skill with her again in the office
Show the athletic trainer how to prompt the skill
Ask her permission to tell the athletic trainer about it
rationales: Being present suits a skill that needs the consultant's expertise at that moment. Her exercises are daily, the consultant comes one day a week, and a prompt is all she needs.
Another lesson suits someone who can't yet do the skill. She does it in seconds and uses it before exams.
She has the skill but forgets it when the exercises begin. The athletic trainer is there each day and can give a brief prompt, within the consent she has given.
Permission comes first when it hasn't been given. Her written consent covers sharing her work between the two professionals.
takeaway: When a client has the skill but not the prompt, equip the professional who is there at the moment.

stem: A consultant is leading a mindfulness program for a company's executives. After ten minutes of attending to the breath, one says, "Three breaths, and I was in my inbox. So I went back to the breath, and there I was in the inbox again. I bet I went back forty times. Then the bell rang." She laughs. "I'm calm, I'm not upset. I'm just obviously no good at it." Several colleagues nod. Which reply best fits what she has said?
options: "Feeling relaxed afterward is welcome, but isn't what we're after."
"Coming back each time is what we're here to practice."
"See if you can let the frustration stay and get curious about it."
"Try following the breath somewhere it's easier to feel."
rationales: This reply corrects the belief that mindfulness is meant to relax. She isn't measuring herself by how relaxed she feels.
She counts each return as a failure. Noticing that the mind has wandered and bringing it back is the skill itself, so the reply reframes what she did forty times as practice.
Getting curious about frustration suits someone who is struggling with it. She says she isn't upset.
Another place to follow the breath suits someone who can't find it. She found it forty times.
takeaway: In mindfulness, noticing that attention has wandered and returning it is the exercise.

stem: In Carron and Spink's team-building framework for exercise groups, components are described as inputs, throughputs, or outputs. At the first class of a new season, an instructor asks members to pick a spot on the studio floor, and she encourages them to keep it all year. Which component of the framework does this strategy target?
options: The group's structure, an input
The group's environment, an input
The group's processes, a throughput
The group's cohesion, an output
rationales: Giving members regular positions of their own is a group structure strategy, alongside roles and norms, and structure is one of the framework's inputs.
The group environment covers distinctiveness, such as a group name or shirts, and closeness. A spot of one's own concerns a member's position within the group.
Group processes cover interaction, such as partner work, shared goals, and sacrifices. Keeping a spot doesn't involve members' working together.
Cohesion is the result the framework aims to produce. Strategies act on the inputs and throughputs that lead to it.
takeaway: In Carron and Spink's framework, positions, roles, and norms belong to group structure.
